summary: EAP Re-authentication Protocol extensions let a peer re-authenticate efficiently with another authenticator, without repeating the full EAP exchange, using an EAP re-authentication server.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone or laptop moves from one wireless access point to another, the network often makes it log in again from scratch, and that is slow. This RFC defines a quicker way: the two sides keep a piece of key material from the last full login, and use it to prove to each other who they are in a single exchange, which also produces a fresh key for the new connection. It works the same whatever authentication method was used originally.

how to re-authenticate with eap without a full exchange

subtitle: A one-round-trip way to re-authenticate with EAP when moving between access points, without repeating the full login.

tldr.problem: When a device moves from one access point to another, repeating the whole EAP exchange takes several round trips and slows the handover down, and some EAP methods cannot re-authenticate at all.
tldr.mechanism: The earlier full EAP exchange leaves a key behind, and from it the peer and a re-authentication server derive a root key, an integrity key that proves possession, and a fresh session key for the new access point, all in one round trip.
tldr.outcome: The peer can re-authenticate in fewer than two round trips against a local server, and the RFC obsoletes RFC 5296 with the same protocol plus fixes for the bootstrapping behaviour and the role of the authenticator.

today:
RFC 6696 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 5296, so it is the current document for the EAP Re-authentication Protocol extensions.

The revision is fully backward compatible with the document it replaces. Its changes are that the home ER server and the EAP server no longer have to be in the same place, that the authenticator and the local ER server are now required to check whether they currently hold the root keys during bootstrapping, and that the authenticator is now recommended rather than merely allowed to start the exchange with an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message. Many other changes were editorial.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol is an authentication framework that supports multiple authentication methods. Its primary purpose is network access authentication, and a key-generating method is used when the lower layer wants to enforce access control. The EAP keying hierarchy defines two keys to be derived by all key-generating EAP methods, the Master Session Key and the Extended MSK. In the most common deployment scenario, an EAP peer and an EAP server authenticate each other through a third party known as the EAP authenticator, and the authenticator or an entity controlled by it enforces access control. After successful authentication the EAP server transports the MSK to the EAP authenticator, and the authenticator and the peer establish Transient Session Keys using the MSK as the authentication key, key derivation key, or key transport key, and use the TSK for per-packet access enforcement.

When a peer moves from one authenticator to another, it is desirable to avoid a full EAP authentication in order to support fast handovers. The full EAP exchange with another run of the EAP method can take several round trips and significant time, which causes increased handover times. Some EAP methods specify the use of state from the initial authentication to optimise re-authentications, but method-specific re-authentication still takes at least two round trips with the original EAP server in most cases, and several methods offer no support for re-authentication at all.

Key sharing across authenticators is sometimes used as a practical way to lower handover times, but then the compromise of one authenticator results in the compromise of key material established via the others. To achieve low latency handovers, a method-independent re-authentication protocol is needed that completes in fewer than two round trips, preferably with a local server.

This document specifies EAP Re-authentication Extensions for efficient re-authentication using EAP. The protocol that uses these extensions is itself the EAP Re-authentication Protocol, and it supports method-independent re-authentication for a peer that has valid, unexpired key material from a previously performed EAP authentication.

The document notes that supporting ERP may require lower-layer specifications to be revised, to allow carrying EAP messages whose code value is higher than 4 and to accommodate the peer-initiated nature of ERP, and it names the Internet Key Exchange protocol as one that must be updated to carry ERP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the device, the access point and the network's authentication server do a full handshake, and that takes several round trips. The point of this RFC is to reuse the key from that handshake so the device can prove itself again in one exchange, no matter which authentication method was used to begin with.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document uses the basic EAP terminology and the EMSK keying hierarchy terminology, and adds a set of terms of its own.

An ER Peer is an EAP peer that supports the EAP Re-authentication Protocol, and every reference to peer in the document means an ER peer unless stated otherwise. An ER Authenticator is an entity that supports the authenticator functionality for EAP re-authentication, and an ER Server is the entity that performs the server portion of the protocol. The ER server may or may not be an EAP server, and it is a logical entity that need not be co-located with, or physically part of, a full EAP server.

ERX denotes the EAP re-authentication extensions and ERP the protocol that uses them. The rRK is the re-authentication Root Key, derived from the EMSK or from the Domain-Specific Root Key. The rIK is the re-authentication Integrity Key, derived from the rRK. The rMSK is the re-authentication MSK, a per-authenticator key derived from the rRK. The keyName-NAI is the name by which the rIK or the DS-rIK is identified: ERP messages are integrity protected with the rIK or the DS-rIK, and the use of one or the other is indicated by the EMSKname, the protocol, which is ERP, and the realm, which indicates the domain name of the ER server. The EMSKname is copied into the username part of the Network Access Identifier.

The domain refers to a key management domain, and the terms home domain and local domain distinguish the originating key management domain that performs the full EAP exchange with the peer from the local domain to which a peer may be attached at a given time.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties are involved and each has a role. The peer is the device. The authenticator is the access point or network edge that enforces access. The ER server is the one that holds the keys and does the real work, and it may be back in the home network or out in the local network where the device has arrived.

sections.title: The ERP Exchange
sections.content:
ERP allows a peer and a server to mutually verify proof of possession of key material from an earlier EAP method run and to establish a security association between the peer and the authenticator. The authenticator acts as a pass-through entity for the re-authentication protocol, in a manner similar to an ordinary EAP authenticator. ERP is a single round-trip exchange between the peer and the server, independent of the lower layer and of the EAP method used during the full EAP exchange. The ER server may be in the home domain or in the same, visited, domain as the peer and the authenticator.

The first time the peer attaches to a network it performs a full EAP exchange with the EAP server, and an MSK is distributed to the EAP authenticator, which the peer and the authenticator use to establish Transient Session Keys as needed. At the time of the initial exchange the peer and the server also derive an EMSK, from which an rRK is derived, either directly or through a Domain-Specific Root Key. The rRK is available only to the peer and the ER server and is never handed to any other entity. An rIK is derived from the rRK, and the peer and the ER server use it to provide proof of possession while performing the ERP exchange; it too is never handed to any other entity.

Two EAP codes are defined for the purpose of EAP re-authentication, EAP-Initiate and EAP-Finish. When the peer identifies a target authenticator that supports EAP re-authentication, it performs an ERP exchange. The exchange may happen when the peer attaches to a new authenticator or before attachment. The peer initiates ERP by itself, and may also do so in response to an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message from the new authenticator, which allows the authenticator to trigger the exchange. The EAP-Finish message can also be used by the authenticator to announce the local domain name.

It is plausible that the authenticator does not know whether the peer supports ERP, or whether the peer has performed a full EAP authentication through another authenticator. The authenticator may initiate the exchange by sending EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start and, if there is no response, send an EAP-Request/Identity, which avoids having two EAP messages in flight at the same time. If the peer does not respond after the necessary retransmissions, the authenticator must initiate EAP by sending an EAP-Request message. When the EAP-Request/Identity times out, the authenticator must not close the connection if an ERP exchange is in progress or has already established a re-authentication MSK.

An authenticator that does not support ERP silently discards EAP-Initiate/Re-auth messages, because the EAP code of those packets is greater than 4. An ERP-capable peer will exhaust its retransmissions and fall back to EAP authentication. A peer that does not support ERP, or that has no unexpired key material from a previous EAP authentication, drops EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start messages.

The peer sends an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message containing the keyName-NAI that identifies the ER server's domain and the rIK used to protect the message, together with a sequence number for replay protection. The message is integrity protected with the rIK. The authenticator uses the realm in the keyName-NAI to send the message to the appropriate ER server, and the server uses the keyName to look up the rIK. After verifying proof of possession of the rIK and the freshness of the message, the server derives an rMSK from the rRK using the sequence number as an input to the key derivation, and updates the expected sequence number to the received number plus one.

In response the server sends an EAP-Finish/Re-auth message, integrity protected with the rIK, and transports the rMSK along with it to the authenticator in a manner similar to the transport of the MSK with EAP-Success in a full exchange. The peer verifies the sequence number and the integrity of the message, and then uses the sequence number in the EAP-Finish/Re-auth message to compute the rMSK. The lower-layer security association protocol is ready to be triggered after that point. The peer may ask for the rMSK lifetime, and the server sends it in the EAP-Finish/Re-auth message. The ER server is located either in the home domain or in the visited domain, and the domain of the ER server is identified by the realm portion of the keyName-NAI.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange is one message from the device to the server and one back. The device proves it still holds the key from the last login by signing the message with a key both sides can compute from it. The server replies with a new key for the new access point, so the device and the access point can start protecting the traffic straight away.

sections.title: The ER Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
Each time the peer re-authenticates to the network, the peer and the authenticator establish an rMSK, which serves the same purposes that the MSK serves after a full EAP authentication. To prove possession of the rRK, the document specifies the derivation of another key, the rIK. These keys are derived from the rRK, and together they constitute the ER key hierarchy: the rRK at the top, the rIK and the rMSKs for the individual authenticators below it.

The rRK is derived from either the EMSK or a DSRK, using a Usage-Specific Root Key derivation as specified in the EMSK keying hierarchy document. The derivation is rRK = KDF(K, S), where K is the EMSK or the DSRK, and S is the rRK label, a null byte, and the length. The rRK label is the 8-bit ASCII string EAP Re-authentication Root Key@ietf.org, assigned from the USRK Key Labels name space. A root key derived from the DSRK is called the DS-rRK.

The rRK has a fixed set of properties. Its length must equal the length of the parent key used to derive it. It is used only as a root key for re-authentication and never to protect data directly, and only for the derivation of the rIK and the rMSK. It must remain on the peer and the server that derived it and must not be transported to any other entity. Its lifetime is never greater than that of its parent key, and it is expired and removed from use when the parent key expires.

The rIK is used for integrity protecting the ERP exchange, which serves as the proof of possession of valid key material from a previous full EAP exchange. It is derived as rIK = KDF(K, S), where K is the rRK and S is the rIK label, a null byte, the cryptosuite and the length. The rIK label is the 8-bit ASCII string Re-authentication Integrity Key@ietf.org. Including the cryptosuite and the length in the input gives cryptographic separation between rIKs of different lengths derived from the same rRK. The rIK must have the same length as the rRK, is used only for authenticating the ERP exchange, must not be used to derive any other keys, must remain on the peer and the server, and is cryptographically separate from any other key derived from the rRK. Its lifetime is never greater than that of the rRK.

The rIK is the key whose possession the peer and the server demonstrate to each other. The peer demonstrates possession by computing the integrity checksum over the EAP-Initiate/Re-auth message, and when it uses the rIK for the first time it may choose the integrity algorithm; the peer and the server must use the same algorithm with a given rIK for all ERP messages protected with that key, and they store the algorithm information after the first use. If the server's policy does not allow the cryptosuite the peer selected, the server must reject the message and should send a list of acceptable cryptosuites in the reply. The rIK length may differ from the key length an integrity algorithm requires, so for hash-based MAC algorithms the key is first hashed to the required length using HMAC, and for cipher-based MAC algorithms with a required key length below 32 octets the rIK is hashed with HMAC-SHA256 and the first k octets of the output are used, while a required key length above 32 octets uses the first k octets of the rIK directly.

The rMSK is derived at the peer and the server and delivered to the authenticator, using rMSK = KDF(K, S), where K is the rRK and S is the rMSK label, a null byte, the sequence number sent by the peer, and the length. The rMSK label is the 8-bit ASCII string Re-authentication Master Session Key@ietf.org, and the sequence number is encoded as a 16-bit number in network byte order. The rMSK must have the same length as the rRK, is delivered to the authenticator and used for the same purposes the MSK serves at an authenticator, is cryptographically separate from any other key derived from the rRK, and has a lifetime less than or equal to that of the rRK. If a new rRK is derived, later rMSKs must come from it, and previously delivered rMSKs may still be used until they expire. A given rMSK must not be shared by multiple authenticators.
sections.plainLanguage: Three keys, each one step down from the last. The root key stays put and is never used to protect anything. The integrity key proves to the server that the device still has the root key. The session key is the one handed to the access point, and there is a separate one for each access point so that leaking one does not expose the others.

sections.title: EAP Codes and Packet Formats
sections.content:
Two EAP codes are defined for the purpose of ERP, EAP-Initiate with value 5 and EAP-Finish with value 6, and the packet format follows the EAP packet format. The Identifier field is one octet. It must be the same if an EAP-Initiate packet is retransmitted because of a timeout while waiting for an EAP-Finish message, and any new, non-retransmission, EAP-Initiate message must use a new Identifier. The Identifier of the EAP-Finish message must match that of the currently outstanding EAP-Initiate message, and a peer or authenticator receiving a mismatch must silently discard the packet. To avoid confusion between new messages and retransmissions the peer must choose an Identifier value different from the previous EAP-Initiate message, especially if that exchange has not finished, and it is recommended that the authenticator clear EAP re-authentication state after 300 seconds.

The Type field indicates that this is an ERP exchange, and two type values are defined for that purpose, Re-auth-Start with type 1 and Re-auth with type 2. The Type-Data field varies with the type.

The EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start packet has type 1, a Reserved field that must be zero, and one or more Type/Value or Type/Length/Value attributes. In a TV payload there is a 1-octet type payload and a value with a type-specific length; in a TLV payload there is a 1-octet type payload and a 1-octet length payload. The domain name is a TLV payload with type 4, and it is to be used as the realm in an NAI; it should be present in an EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message. Channel binding information may also be included.

The EAP-Initiate/Re-auth packet has type 2 and carries a flags octet, a sequence number, one or more TVs or TLVs, a cryptosuite and an authentication tag. The R flag is set to zero and ignored on reception. The B flag is the bootstrapping flag, and when it is on the message is a bootstrap message. The L flag requests the key lifetimes from the server. The remaining 5 bits are set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

The SEQ field is an unsigned 16-bit sequence number used for replay protection, encoded in network byte order and initialised to zero every time a new rRK is derived. The keyName-NAI is carried in a TLV payload with type 1. The NAI is variable in length and does not exceed 253 octets; the EMSKname is in the username part, encoded in hexadecimal, and is 64 bits long, so the username portion takes up 16 octets. If the rIK is derived from the EMSK the realm part of the NAI is the home domain name, and if it is derived from a DSRK the realm part is the domain name used in the derivation of the DSRK. Exactly one keyName-NAI attribute must be present.

The Cryptosuite field indicates the integrity algorithm used for ERP. Three are specified: 0 is reserved, 1 is HMAC-SHA256-64, 2 is HMAC-SHA256-128 and 3 is HMAC-SHA256-256. HMAC-SHA256-128 is mandatory to implement and should be enabled in the default configuration. The Authentication Tag field holds the integrity checksum over the ERP packet, excluding the tag field itself, and its length is given by the cryptosuite.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new EAP message types are added, both with numbers above 4, which is why a lower layer that only knows the old codes will ignore them. The message from the device carries a one-off counter, a name that says which server and which key to use, and a checksum that proves the device holds that key.

sections.title: Replay Protection and Channel Binding
sections.content:
For replay protection of ERP messages, a sequence number associated with the rIK is used. The sequence number is maintained by the peer and the server and is initialised to zero when the rIK is generated. The peer increments it by one after it sends an ERP message, and the server sets the expected sequence number to the received number plus one after verifying the validity of the received message and before responding to it.

Channel binding is a separate mechanism that can be used to verify that the authenticator is claiming the same identity to both parties. The peer and the authenticator demonstrate possession of the same key material without disclosing it, as part of the lower-layer secure association protocol. Channel binding with ERP may be used to verify the consistency of the identities exchanged when the identities used in the lower layer differ from those exchanged within the AAA protocol, and the authenticator may include channel binding information so that the server can check this. The authenticator may also include it in the EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start message.
sections.plainLanguage: Two checks stop a captured message from being reused. A counter number travels with every message and the receiver remembers the last one it accepted, so a replayed message is refused. Channel binding is a way of confirming that the access point gives the server the same identity it gives the device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document sets out the security properties the protocol is designed to provide.

Mutual authentication of the peer and the server comes from both parties needing the key material that resulted from a previous EAP exchange in order to derive the required keys, and from the re-authentication messages being integrity protected so that the peer and the server can verify each other. The peer and the authenticator authenticate each other in the secure association protocol executed by the lower layer, as in a regular EAP exchange, and the peer and the authenticator demonstrate possession of the same key material without disclosing it.

ERP results in strong, fresh keys that are unique for the given session. An rMSK is always derived on demand when the peer requires a key with a new authenticator, and the derivation ensures that the compromise of one rMSK does not result in the compromise of another.

The scope of the keys is well defined. The rRK and the rIK are never shared with any entity and always remain on the peer and the server, and the rMSK is provided only to the authenticator through which the peer performs the exchange; no other authenticator is authorised to use it.

The peer and the server derive the keys independently using parameters known to each entity, and the AAA server sends the DSRK of a domain to the corresponding local ER server over the AAA protocol, and the ER server sends the rMSK to the authenticator the same way. The document is explicit about the limits: compromise of the DSRK results in compromise of all keys derived from it, and there is no forward secrecy within ERP, so compromise of a DSRK retroactively compromises all ERP keys. It is recommended that the AAA protocol be protected using IPsec or TLS so that the keys are protected in transit, noting that keys may still be exposed to AAA proxies along the way.

The home EAP server must not hand out a given DSRK to a local domain server more than once, unless it can verify that the entity receiving it the second time is the same entity that received it originally.

On algorithm selection, the document notes that a full negotiation of algorithms cannot be provided in a single round-trip protocol, so while the protocol provides algorithm agility it does not provide true negotiation. The cryptosuite is included in the exchange by the peer and confirmed by the server, and the server may reject the cryptosuite the peer selected and provide alternatives. When a suitable rIK is not available for the peer, the alternatives may be sent in an unprotected fashion, and the peer may retry with one of the allowed cryptosuites, but in that case any modification to the list in transit goes undetected.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is careful about what each key can be used for, and the document says plainly what it does not protect against. There is no forward secrecy: if the domain key is stolen later, everything derived from it can be worked out. And because the whole exchange fits in one round trip, the server cannot negotiate the algorithm properly, it can only accept or reject the one the device picked.

messages.label: EAP-Initiate/Re-auth-Start
messages.note: The authenticator offers ERP and may include the local domain name.

messages.label: EAP-Initiate/Re-auth
messages.note: Carries the keyName-NAI, a sequence number and a checksum made with the rIK.

messages.label: AAA(rMSK, EAP-Finish/Re-auth)
messages.note: The server checks the rIK, derives the rMSK and sends it onwards.

messages.label: EAP-Finish/Re-auth
messages.note: Integrity protected with the rIK; the peer derives the same rMSK.

root.label: rRK
root.note: Derived from the EMSK or the DSRK; never leaves the peer and the server

children.label: rIK
children.note: Proves possession during the exchange; never leaves the peer and the server

children.label: rMSK1 ... rMSKn
children.note: One per authenticator, delivered to that authenticator only

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Must match the outstanding EAP-Initiate message, and be new for each new message.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the whole packet.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The B flag marks a bootstrap message and the L flag requests the key lifetimes.

fields.name: SEQ
fields.desc: An unsigned 16-bit sequence number used for replay protection.

viz.caption: THE SECURITY PROPERTIES ERP AIMS FOR (RFC 6696)

items.title: Mutual authentication
items.text: Both sides need the key material from the earlier EAP exchange, and the messages are integrity protected.

items.title: Fresh session keys
items.text: An rMSK is derived on demand for each new authenticator, so compromising one does not compromise another.

items.title: Limited key scope
items.text: The rRK and rIK never leave the peer and the server; an rMSK goes only to the authenticator it was derived for.

items.title: Replay detection
items.text: A sequence number tied to the rIK is kept by both sides and advanced on every message.

items.title: No forward secrecy
items.text: Compromise of a DSRK retroactively compromises every key derived from it.
